from.why: Even with cognitive work nearly free, engine development (hot-fire campaigns, turbopump failures), pad construction (2-4 years) and flight-test learning set a floor of about 4-5 years. AI's best case removes about a year, and only programs started after AI adoption (2027-28 in S2) benefit. The realistic path is a derivative built around an existing engine family: LandSpace's Zhuque-3 (TQ-12-family methalox engines from Zhuque-2) hopped in Jan 2024, reached orbit Dec 3 2025 and landed its first stage on its second flight, Aug 18 2026 (Wikipedia), on roughly a four-year derivative timeline without AI help (general). Clean-sheet multipliers of 0.8-0.9x (S2) and 0.7-0.8x (S3) on such a timeline give about 3.2-3.6 years in S2, so Speculative, and 2.8-3.2 years in S3, so Low. FAA licensing reform and AI-run test stands help U.S. entrants but are not gates for every entrant.

add_nodes.title: 300+ fully reusable heavy launches a year
add_nodes.description: Fully reusable heavy launchers fly 300 or more orbital missions in one calendar year, three times the 100-flight milestone.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. Starship flew 5 times in 2025 and 3 times in 2026 to Oct 7. Approved site caps total about 145 Starship launches a year: Starbase 25 (FAA, May 2025), LC-39A 44 (Jan 2026) and SLC-37 76 (Dec 2025). Mach33's reference case has about 90 Starship flights in 2028 and about 516,000 t to orbit in 2040, 456,000 t of it SpaceX's own (Launch Keystone, Sep 2026), which implies thousands of flights a year by 2040. A permit application for a haul road, a Gulf wharf and canal dredging at SpaceX's planned Pecan Island, Louisiana site was reportedly filed on Sep 29, 2026 (unconfirmed by SpaceX or an agency); it covers construction only.
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor. 300 flights a year is about one a day. Approved Starship caps total about 145 a year (Starbase 25, LC-39A 44, SLC-37 76), and they come from completed reviews. Caps for 300+ need new site environmental assessments or impact statements (EIS median about 2.2 years, plus litigation risk) that are not yet filed. EO 14335 speeds reviews. It sets no caps. New pads take 2-4 years each, and large transformers take 128-160 weeks. Demand comes from Starlink V3 and later, orbital compute (capability-compute-launch-demand) and lunar tanker campaigns. Chain (S2): 100+ flights 2030 -> new site reviews filed 2027-28 and decided 2029-30 -> new pads and raised caps 2031-32 -> 300+ flights 2033. S3 2032: cadence runs a year ahead and compute demand is stronger. S1 2034: the plateau weakens compute demand, and Starlink alone needs far fewer flights. AI moves cadence by months through anomaly closure and range scheduling. Mach33's reference tonnage (about 35,400 t in 2029, or 240-320 flights at 112-150 t each) runs well above approved caps, so it cannot date this node. S4 gets no year or band: approvals, airspace and environmental caps bind, and robots do not touch them. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). Bands (judgment): Medium by 2035 in S2-S4 under the regulatory cap, because no review covering 300+ launches a year is filed; raise S2-S4 to High once one is. S1 Low.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Starship has never met a yearly flight plan, and each failure grounds the fleet for weeks to months. Airspace closures, local opposition and litigation can cap cadence below what vehicles and pads allow.
add_nodes.signpost: A filed environmental review covering 300 or more Starship launches a year across sites (raises S2-S4 to High); 150 or more Starship flights in 2031; a fourth Starship launch site approved; per-site caps raised above 100 a year.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. Approvals bind: caps for 300+ a year need new site reviews that are not yet filed, so S2-S4 are Medium by 2035. S4 adds nothing because approvals, airspace and environmental caps do not compress.

add_nodes.title: Starship internal cost under $100 per kg
add_nodes.description: SpaceX's internal cost to put a kilogram in low orbit on Starship falls below $100/kg, a third of the $300/kg milestone. Development, pads and factories are excluded.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. Flight 14 (Sep 28, 2026) cost about $4,915/kg with both stages expended (Mach33). Mach33's base case: $656/kg in 2027, about $300/kg in 2028, 8.9 flights per stack in 2029 and 18 in 2030, $13/kg in 2035 and $10/kg in 2040 (Launch Keystone v1.3, Sep 23, 2026).
add_nodes.premise_tier: n/a (exogenous physical clock: not an AI-math implication, so the P7 Speculative default does not apply)
add_nodes.why: Not an AI-math implication: an exogenous physical anchor set by flights per stack, payload per flight and production learning (Mach33 splits the early decline 56% reuse, 32% payload, 12% learning). A $85-100M stack flying 18 times with $4M of operations and 112 t of payload costs about $80-85/kg (estimate), so the threshold needs ships flying about 10 times or more as well as boosters flying 20-30 times. Mach33's base reaches 18 flights per stack in 2030, and its 0.85 learning rate per doubling of delivered mass takes the $143M stack of 2028 to about $85-100M by 2030 (estimate), so Mach33 crosses $100/kg in 2030. The model dates $300/kg a year after Mach33 (2029 against 2028); the same lag puts $100/kg at 2031. Ship reuse at that count needs the rapidly reusable heat shield, a hard prerequisite (hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield: S1 2031, S2 2030, S3 2029), so S1 follows in 2032. Band by 2031: S2 Low because the heat shield is only Medium by 2031 and the chain has no slack; S3 and S4 Medium with two years of heat-shield slack; S1 Low. S4 gets no credit: reuse and payload set cost, and refurbishment robots trim an operating cost that is already a small share. Mach33 projections are a single commercial forecaster's model estimates, not independent research (an equity disclosure was reported on its pages; unverified here). High by 2035 in every scenario (judgment): Mach33's 2035 base sits about 8x below the threshold, so only a failure of ship reuse keeps cost above it. That High holds only while the heat shield is High by 2035.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: If tiles are a dead end for ship reuse, ships stay near single use and cost stays near $300/kg (a $40M ship over 150 t, plus booster and operations; estimate). Internal cost also does not reach customers: Mach33's median 2035 customer revenue is about $945/kg.
add_nodes.signpost: Disclosed ship flights per stack above 10; payload per flight near 150 t; cost estimates below $150/kg. SpaceX does not report cost per kg, so the signpost rests on estimates; Mach33's $13/kg for 2035 is one commercial model.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. The launch clock runs without AI math, so S2-S4 share the year and S1 follows its later heat shield. High by 2035 holds only while hyper-rapid-reuse-heatshield is High by 2035; if the entry branch keeps it Medium, this node drops to Medium in all four scenarios. S4 gets no credit.

add_nodes.title: Leading firms halve development cycles
add_nodes.description: A leading firm completes a launch vehicle, crew or cargo vehicle, or new large spacecraft program, whose own pre-2027 comparable took 3 years or more, in at most half that time, with a published schedule analysis. Repeat constellation generations do not count (see physclock-satellite-gen-cadence); typical programs are covered by capability-program-cycle-compression.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. Comparable programs today: clean-sheet launchers take 5-13 years, new engines 6-13 years and human rating about 6 years (model gate table); Starship SN8-SN15 flew in 147 days with human crews. Only a few thousand humanoids do paid work, most need teleoperation (IFR, Sep 30, 2026), and none do flight-hardware assembly.
add_nodes.why: Amdahl with physics held fixed (s4-embodied): 2035 ceilings are about 42-52% in S2 (judgment from the model's program shares), 56% in S3, 58-62% in S4 for typical and leading programs, and 66-67% at robot-first firms. Realized gains run below ceilings: 40-48% in S3, 42-54% in S4 typical and leading, 50-58% at robot-first firms. These ranges apply to programs run under that year's conditions, so a program finished in 2034 ran under 2032-34 conditions. Chain (S4): robots in paid flight-hardware work at leading firms 2030-31 (robo-aerospace-tolerance-work) -> processes requalified by 2032 (6-24 months each; early adopters dip first) -> program started 2032 -> completed 2034 under 2032-34 conditions, with a robot-first realized gain of about 45-54% -> published analysis 2034. S3: programs run under 2033-35 conditions realize 40-48%, so halving sits above the range and first becomes credible in 2035. S1 and S2 stay after 2035 because their ceilings sit near or below 50%. S4 credit passes all four tests: integration, test and fabrication labor bind at the firm; robots are useful there from 2030-31; no hard prerequisite lands later; and general-purpose robots go beyond the specialized test stands already in S3. Band: the P7 default (Speculative) holds for S1 and S2. S3 is Low and S4 Medium (judgment), because 50% sits inside the S4 robot-first range and above S3's. S4 Medium is a ceiling: it falls to Low if robo-24x7-integration-test is below High in S4 by 2035. Bands are judgments.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: At a robot-first firm in 2035, physics time constants, reliability statistics and institutions still make up about 44% of the remaining critical path, so one anomaly or a requalification dip erases the margin. Firms may spend the gain on scope, and attribution to AI and robots will be disputed.
add_nodes.signpost: A firm reports a new vehicle or large spacecraft program at half the duration of its own predecessor; humanoids in paid aerospace integration and test; the first robotic-process requalification for flight hardware.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension. S4 reaches it about a year before S3 (2034 against 2035) and is Medium against Low, carried by robot-first integration and test on requalified processes.

Advocate's S2 2035/Low, S3 2033/Medium, S4 2032/High and the soft edge from physclock-satellite-gen-cadence rejected: they rested on satellite generations, which the narrowed scope excludes.

add_nodes.title: A launcher or large spacecraft engineered mostly by AI flies
add_nodes.description: A launch-vehicle stage, a crew or cargo vehicle, or a non-constellation spacecraft over 5 t dry mass, whose design analyses, trades and verification artifacts were mostly AI-generated (with human review), flies and operates. Constellation satellites are covered by capability-ai-native-spacecraft.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Not yet. AI-generated engine and structural geometry and agentic chip design exist piecemeal. SpaceX owns a frontier lab (SpaceXAI) and flies Starlink V3 at about 2 t. Constellation satellites do not count here.
add_nodes.why: Second-generation step: the AI-native process (capability-ai-native-spacecraft) applied to a stage, a crew or cargo vehicle, or a large non-constellation spacecraft, where hot fire, integration and qualification bind whoever does the design. Constellation satellites are excluded so that one AI-designed Starlink generation cannot satisfy both nodes. Chain (S3): AI-native smallsat flies 2029 -> stage or vehicle design starts 2029 -> a four-year derivative program at 0.7-0.75x flies 2032. S2: 0.8-0.85x on the same base gives 3.2-3.4 years, so 2033. S1: the smallsat flies in 2031, so a large system follows after 2035. A clean-sheet program (5-13 years at 0.7-0.8x in S3) would land later; derivatives set the date. Band: the P7 default (Speculative) holds for S1. S2 Low and S3 Medium by 2035 (judgment): hot fire and flight tests are unchanged, and firms may not disclose what share AI produced. S4 equals S3: qualification, flight tests and disclosure bind, and integration robots add months at most. Bands are judgments.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Large systems carry more legacy process and liability, and firms may not publish what share AI produced. A launch stage is bound by hot fire and flight tests whoever designs it.
add_nodes.signpost: A launch firm or vehicle maker publishes AI-generated verification evidence for a new stage, vehicle or large spacecraft before flight, then reports flight success.
add_nodes.note_2035: New in the 2035 extension, scoped to stages, vehicles and large non-constellation spacecraft. S4 equals S3 because hot fire, flight tests and disclosure bind; robots on the build add months at most.

Advocate's S2 High rejected (rested on a SpaceX satellite generation, now out of scope); its robot soft edges added as mechanism, with no S4 credit.

patch.thesis: If research-grade AI math reaches outside engineers in 2027 (base case), on-demand analysis is routine in space engineering by 2028. Tests, factories and launches run on physical time, so schedules shrink 20-30% by 2031 and about a third by 2035. Robots (S4) add little before 2032; robot-first firms approach half on programs started after 2032.
